newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn slams "crazy" talk of mass Bosnian expulsions.
newsitem.headline: Bonn slams "crazy" talk of mass Bosnian expulsions.

text.p: Germany on Thursday rejected U.S. criticism of its drive to deport wartime refugees to Bosnia and urged the Bosnian authorities to do everything they could to help exiles return quickly and peacefully to their homeland.

Interior Minister Manfred Kanther, asked to comment on a U.S. State Department warning against early repatriation, said talk of mass deportations of Bosnians from Germany was "crazy" and anyone doing so was engaging in polemics.
Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel joined Kanther in rejecting outside advice on the refugee issue and appealed to the Bosnian leadership to stop bickering and rebuild their country.
The sharp rebuffs came after State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns called on Germany not to send back Bosnians who would be in a minority in their home regions.

Burns' remarks fanned a controversy over the refugees in Germany, where Kanther's hard line on expelling them has come under fire from the United Nations, opposition leaders and colleagues like Kinkel and Defence Minister Volker Ruehe.
"There are no mass deportations," Kanther told journalists in Berlin. "Whoever is crazy enough to talk about mass deportations -- whoever he is -- only wants to blow the issue up into polemics."

There are still some 300,000 Bosnian refugees in Germany, most of them Moslems driven out of areas now ruled by Serbs, and officials from Germany's 16 cash-strapped regional states want them to go home soon.
But Kanther's critics say state officials have been needlessly harsh, sending back Moslems to areas now dominated by Serbs or forcing pregnant women and heart patients onto planes to leave.
Kanther said Germany had deported only 191 Bosnians since last October and about 30,000 had gone home voluntarily according to a German-Bosnian repatriation agreement.
Noting Germany had taken in about 60 percent of all Bosnian refugees, he added: "We don't need any third party to give us marks for our performance."

Bavaria, which with Berlin has been among the most active of German states in deporting Bosnians, retorted that it only sent back refugees to Sarajevo, where the Bosnian government made final decisions on where to settle them.

"(Deportations) are not made to defined regions of origin, but to Sarajevo, where Bosnian authories who have been informed in advance (of their arrival) take over their further distribution," state interior minister Guenter Beckstein said.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees office in Bonn echoed Burns' warning, saying: "The repatriation plan as it now stands does not correspond to the reality in Bosnia. People there are threatened in life and limb."

In his appeal to Bosnia's tripartite presidency, Kinkel said the Balkan state was far behind schedule in setting up the civil institutions and rebuilding the economy as called for in the Dayton peace accord.

"The pictures and reports of burning houses, dubious court actions and public media that spread prejudice and dislike rather than reconciliation all do unspeakable harm to a task that I hoped would bring us together," he said.
In a separate statement, Kinkel added that international support for Bosnia would crumble if it turned out that the country's leaders were not implementing the Dayton accord.

Kinkel stressed Germany did not want to "dump the refugees in Sarajevo and leave them to an uncertain future" but added: "There can be no return of civil war refugees on a silver platter. A fully-insured return is also impossible."

Defending the German repatriation drive, Kanther said he and state interior ministers had drawn up clear guidelines for expulsions that made exceptions for cases like youths in vocational training, traumatised and ill people or old people with relatives living in Germany.
"During the period when Germany took in 60 percent of all war refugees from Bosnia, I didn't see any others being as ready to help," he remarked.
